title: The silver (conformed) layer
summary: Turning raw deliveries into typed, deduplicated, conformed entities: CDC application with MERGE, history, quality gates, quarantine and incremental processing.

blocks.text: Silver is where data becomes trustworthy. It answers *what is true about each business entity*: one customer, one order, one product, with consistent types, keys and codes regardless of which source said it. Silver is still mostly source- or entity-shaped, not report-shaped; report shaping belongs in gold (chapter 15).
14.1 Typing and cleaning

items: **Cast explicitly** with safe-cast functions (`TRY_CAST` in Snowflake and Spark SQL) so one bad value does not fail the batch, then count the NULLs it produced.
**Rename** to a house convention (snake_case, `_at` for timestamps, `_id` for natural keys, `is_` for booleans).
**Normalise units and time zones**: store timestamps in UTC (`TIMESTAMP_NTZ` holding UTC, or a time-zone-aware type) and amounts with an explicit currency column.
**Standardise empties**: empty strings, `'N/A'` and `'null'` strings become real NULLs; trim whitespace on keys.
Do not invent values. Defaulting a missing country to `'US'` hides a data problem instead of surfacing it.

blocks.text: 14.2 Deduplication: latest record per key

Duplicates arrive constantly: at-least-once delivery from Kafka, overlapping API pages, re-sent files, CDC snapshots overlapping with the change stream. The standard pattern ranks records per key by a reliable ordering column and keeps the first.

blocks.title: Latest per key (Snowflake, with QUALIFY)
blocks.text:
SELECT
  raw:id::NUMBER                AS order_id,
  raw:status::STRING            AS status,
  TRY_TO_DECIMAL(raw:amount::STRING, 18, 2) AS amount,
  raw:updated_at::TIMESTAMP_NTZ AS updated_at,
  _source_ts,
  _ingested_at
FROM bronze.shop__orders
WHERE _ingested_at > :last_watermark
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
  PARTITION BY raw:id::NUMBER
  ORDER BY _source_ts DESC, _lsn DESC, _ingested_at DESC
) = 1;

blocks.title: The same in Spark SQL (portable subquery form)

blocks.text: Ordering by `_ingested_at` alone is wrong for CDC: two changes in the same batch share an ingestion time, and a late-arriving older change would win. Order by the source's commit position (LSN, binlog position, SCN) or source timestamp first, and add tie-breakers so the result is deterministic.

Exact duplicates (same key and same payload) can be removed by hashing the payload. Near-duplicates (same real-world entity, different keys, such as one person with two CRM records) are an entity-resolution problem, solved by matching rules or a mastering tool and recorded as a key-mapping table.
14.3 Conforming keys and codes
Conforming makes data from different sources line up. It is where silver earns the name *conformed* and where conformed dimensions for gold (chapter 8) are born.

Example
Silver solution
rows: Different keys for the same entity
Shop customer 812 is CRM contact C-0091
Key-mapping table to one enterprise customer key

blocks.text: 14.4 Applying CDC with MERGE

To build the current state of a source table from a change stream, take the latest change per key in the new batch and MERGE it into the silver table, honouring deletes. Run against an Iceberg or Delta table, this produces row-level writes (copy-on-write or merge-on-read, chapter 23).

blocks.title: CDC upsert with deletes (Spark SQL on Iceberg)
blocks.text:
MERGE INTO silver.orders t
USING (
  SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT c.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id
                              ORDER BY lsn DESC) AS rn
    FROM staged_order_changes c
  ) WHERE rn = 1
) s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'd' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.lsn > t.lsn THEN UPDATE SET
  t.status = s.status,
  t.amount = s.amount,
  t.updated_at = s.updated_at,
  t.lsn = s.lsn
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'd' THEN INSERT
  (order_id, status, amount, updated_at, lsn)
  VALUES (s.order_id, s.status, s.amount, s.updated_at, s.lsn);

items: **One source row per key** per MERGE, or the engine raises a multiple-match error.
**Guard with the ordering column** (`s.lsn > t.lsn`) so replaying an old batch cannot overwrite newer state. That makes the MERGE idempotent.
**Soft deletes** (`is_deleted = true`, `deleted_at`) instead of physical deletes keep the fact that a record existed, which gold sometimes needs; erasure requirements may force hard deletes.
To keep history instead of only current state, feed the same changes into an SCD2 table (chapter 9) or keep both a current table and a history table.

blocks.text: 14.5 Quality checks and quarantine
Silver is the main quality gate. Decide per rule what happens on failure:

head: Severity
Example rule
Action
rows: Primary key unique and not null
Fail the run; do not publish partial silver
Route the row to a quarantine table, load the rest
Load and alert the owning team

blocks.text: A **quarantine table** has the same columns as the target plus the failed rule names, the batch id and a timestamp. Quarantined rows are reprocessed after the fix, either automatically on the next run or by an explicit replay. Track quarantine volume as a metric; a quarantine that only grows is a silent data-loss channel.

Write-audit-publish: write the new batch to a staging branch or table, run the checks, and only then swap or fast-forward it into the published table. Iceberg branches, Delta clones, Snowflake zero-copy clones and dbt's build order with tests all support variations of this pattern (chapter 33).
14.6 Incremental processing

Full rebuilds of silver are simple and correct but scale with total history; incremental processing scales with change volume. A 5 TB order history with 2 GB of daily change is a 2,500x difference in data processed.

items: **Watermark on ingestion time**: process bronze rows with `_ingested_at` above the last successful high-water mark. Robust against late business timestamps.
**Lookback window**: reprocess the last N hours or days to catch late or replayed records; requires idempotent MERGE.
**Change feeds**: Iceberg incremental reads between snapshots, Delta change data feed or Snowflake streams deliver exactly what changed since the last read.
**Periodic full refresh**: schedule an occasional rebuild to correct drift from logic changes.

blocks.title: dbt incremental silver model (Snowflake adapter)
Unifying customers across shop and CRM
blocks.text: An online retailer had customer data in its shop database (CDC) and in a CRM (nightly API pull). Silver built `silver.customers_shop` and `silver.customers_crm` as typed current-state tables, then an `int_customer_key_map` matching on normalised email and a manual override table, and finally a conformed `silver.customers` keyed by an enterprise customer id.
items: Matching rules were versioned and tested like any other model
Unmatched records were kept with their source key rather than dropped
Gold's `dim_customer` read only the conformed table

blocks.title: Silver for a payments feed
blocks.text: Payment events arrive at least once from a provider's webhooks, sometimes out of order, with states created, authorised, captured, refunded and failed. Design the silver tables (current state and history), the deduplication ordering, the quality rules with their severity, and the incremental strategy including how far back to look.
hints: Is the provider's event timestamp or your ingestion time the right ordering column?
What should happen when a refunded event arrives before captured?

items: Silver is typed, deduplicated and conformed entity data, not report-shaped data.
Deduplicate with ROW_NUMBER over a reliable source ordering column plus deterministic tie-breakers.
Conforming keys, codes and time zones is what makes cross-source analysis possible.
Apply CDC with one row per key, an ordering guard and explicit delete handling to stay idempotent.
Gate quality with blocking, quarantine and warning rules, and process incrementally with a lookback.

blocks.q: Two CDC updates for the same order arrive in one batch. Which ordering picks the correct latest version?
blocks.explain: Both changes may share an ingestion time; the source commit position reflects the true order. Ingestion time is a tie-breaker, not the primary ordering.

blocks.q: Why include `s.lsn > t.lsn` in the MERGE update condition?
options: So replaying an older batch cannot overwrite newer state, making reruns idempotent
To allow multiple source rows per key
Because MERGE requires a non-key condition
blocks.explain: The guard ensures only newer changes win. Without it, a replayed or late batch would roll rows back to older values.

blocks.q: An amount field cannot be parsed for 0.1% of rows. What is the usual silver behaviour?
options: Route the rows to a quarantine table with the failed rule and load the rest
blocks.explain: Row-level problems go to quarantine so the rest of the data stays fresh and nothing is silently lost. Defaulting to zero falsifies totals.

blocks.q: Why add a lookback window to incremental processing?
options: To catch late-arriving or replayed records that fell behind the watermark
Because MERGE cannot run without one
blocks.explain: Records can arrive late or be re-delivered. Reprocessing a recent window, with an idempotent MERGE, catches them. It slightly increases cost rather than reducing it.
